factor_verdicts.reason: The delayed Enactor overwriting a newer plan with an older one is a direct, well-evidenced trigger of the outage; the one-time pre-apply check was the gap that allowed it.
Clean-up deleting the plan that had become active directly produced the empty DNS record, as stated in the report.
Automation did not repair the empty or inconsistent state and manual intervention was required, which prolonged recovery; evidence is explicit.
EC2 DWFM and other services depending on DynamoDB in us-east-1 spread the impact; evidence supports it. Cross-region dependencies from #12 are folded in here.

factor_verdicts.reason: Report states there was no established recovery procedure for DWFM lease recovery and engineers proceeded cautiously through multiple mitigation steps, slowing recovery.
Lease re-establishment timing out and queuing retries without forward progress is clearly stated and delayed EC2 launch recovery.
Health checks marking instances unhealthy before network state propagated is explicitly described and caused capacity removal.
Alternating results overloading the health check subsystem and triggering automatic AZ failover that removed capacity is explicitly described.
Network Manager backlog slowed propagation, leaving new instances without connectivity until 10:36 AM, per the report.
Throttling and host restarts were recovery actions that cleared queues and limited damage; the throttling side effects are a minor trade-off, not a cause of the failure or delay.

factors.factor: Race condition between DNS Enactors: a delayed Enactor applied an older plan after a newer plan had already been applied, overwriting it
factors.evidence: "the first (delayed) Enactor applied its much older plan to the regional DynamoDB endpoint, overwriting the newer plan."

factors.factor: Plan clean-up process deleted the active plan, leaving the regional DNS record empty
factors.evidence: "The second Enactor's clean-up process then deleted this older plan because it was many generations older than the plan it had just applied. As this plan was deleted, all IP addresses for the regional endpoint were immediately removed, leaving an empty DNS record."

factors.factor: Automation lacked safeguards to detect and repair an empty DNS record or an inconsistent state, requiring manual intervention
factors.evidence: "Because the active plan was deleted, the system was left in an inconsistent state in which no DNS Enactor could apply subsequent plan updates. The automation did not repair the record. Manual operator intervention was required."

factors.factor: Services in us-east-1 and other Regions had hard dependencies on DynamoDB and other us-east-1 components (e.g., DWFM state checks, Redshift's IAM API call for user group resolution, and the Support Center account metadata subsystem), so the DynamoDB failure cascaded widely and spread impact beyond the Region.
factors.evidence: "EC2 launches depend on two subsystems... DropletWorkflow Manager (DWFM)... DWFM state checks began to fail, because the process depends on DynamoDB." and "Redshift used an IAM API in us-east-1 to resolve user groups." | "Redshift customers in all Regions could not use IAM user credentials for queries, because Redshift used an IAM API in us-east-1 to resolve user groups." and "an account metadata subsystem returned invalid responses that blocked legitimate users."

factors.factor: No established operational recovery procedure for DWFM lease re-establishment after DynamoDB recovery, prolonging EC2 launch failures
factors.evidence: "There was no established operational recovery procedure for this situation, and engineers took care not to cause further issues while attempting multiple mitigation steps."

factors.factor: DWFM lease re-establishment at fleet scale timed out and queued retries without forward progress
factors.evidence: "Because of the large number of droplets, establishing new leases took long enough that the work timed out before it completed. Additional work was queued to retry, and DWFM was unable to make forward progress in recovering leases."

factors.factor: Network Load Balancer health checks marked new instances unhealthy before network state propagated, causing alternating health results and removal of capacity
factors.evidence: "the health check subsystem brought new EC2 instances into service before their network state had fully propagated, so health checks failed even when NLB nodes and targets were healthy. Health checks alternated between failing and healthy"

factors.factor: Automatic health check failover amplified load on the health check subsystem, removing capacity from service
factors.evidence: "The alternating results increased load on the health check subsystem, which degraded, delayed health checks and triggered automatic AZ DNS failover."

factors.factor: Network Manager backlog from the delayed EC2 recovery slowed propagation of network configuration to new instances
factors.evidence: "Network Manager began propagating network configurations to newly launched instances, with a significant backlog from the delay."

action_items.action: Add a fix so that a DNS Enactor cannot apply a plan older than the currently active plan, enforcing plan generation ordering atomically at the Route53 transaction level rather than relying on a one-time pre-apply check.

Change the plan clean-up process so it never deletes the currently active plan or any plan that could still be referenced, and add a guard that refuses clean-up when the regional endpoint record would become empty.
Implement automated detection and self-repair for an empty or inconsistent regional DNS record, including an alarm that pages on-call when any endpoint has zero healthy IP addresses.
Write and rehearse a runbook for restoring the DynamoDB regional DNS state and re-enabling DNS Enactors, so manual recovery does not depend on ad hoc operator decisions.
Create a documented operational recovery procedure for DWFM lease re-establishment after a dependency outage, including fleet-scale staged lease recovery and throttling guidance.

Make DWFM lease re-establishment resilient to fleet-scale timeouts by batching work, applying exponential backoff, and ensuring retries make forward progress rather than accumulating queued duplicates.
Reduce EC2 control-plane dependency on DynamoDB in us-east-1 by caching droplet state or adding a fallback path so that a DynamoDB outage does not cause lease expiry across the fleet.
Gate NLB health check admission of new EC2 instances until network configuration propagation is confirmed, so instances are not marked unhealthy and removed from DNS due to propagation lag.
Add rate limiting and circuit breaking to the NLB health check subsystem so that alternating health results cannot overload health checks and trigger cascading automatic AZ failover.
Add alarms on Network Manager propagation backlog and latency so backlog growth is detected and acted on before new instances fail to get connectivity.

Audit services in other Regions (for example Redshift IAM user group resolution and Support Center account metadata) for hard dependencies on us-east-1 and add regional fallbacks or cached credential resolution.
